sources.title: Concurrent transfer candidate executable boundary and concurrency test

claims.text: The Java Lock API describes locks as controlling access to shared resources, recommends lock/try/finally/unlock, and specifies successful lock/unlock memory synchronization semantics; the candidate keeps balance reads and writes under the account lock and releases in finally.

Oracle's concurrency tutorial demonstrates deadlock when two threads each hold one resource while waiting for the other; the candidate removes that call-direction-dependent cycle for a pair of accounts by requiring one stable account-id lock order on every path.

The candidate compiles and the executable test verifies successful and insufficient-funds transfers, self-transfer, duplicate-id rejection, overflow-before-write atomicity, and two concurrent opposite-direction transfer loops completing without deadlock while preserving total balance.

validation.command: tmpdir=$(mktemp -d); awk 'BEGIN { in_code = 0 } /^```java$/ { in_code = 1; next } in_code && /^```$/ { exit } in_code { print }' review/candidates/answers/cq_concurrent_transfer_a35181e0.md > $tmpdir/TransferService.java; javac -encoding UTF-8 -d $tmpdir $tmpdir/TransferService.java review/evidence/tests/cq_concurrent_transfer_a35181e0/TransferServiceTest.java; java -ea -cp $tmpdir TransferServiceTest

boundary_tests.expected: success updates both balances; insufficient funds returns false and leaves both unchanged

boundary_tests.case: self transfer, duplicate ids, and target overflow
boundary_tests.expected: self transfer is a no-op; distinct accounts sharing an id are rejected; overflow throws before either balance changes
two 10,000-iteration workers complete within timeout, preserve total balance, and return both accounts to their initial balances
